one_liner: Closed-source parallel sparse LU solver for SPICE circuit matrices; first-party claims >3x over KLU sequential, >25x at 16 threads.
what_it_does: CKTSO (successor to NICSLU from the same author) solves the sparse linear systems inside SPICE Newton-Raphson loops: analyse once, factorize with pivoting, then refactorize without pivoting and solve many times as values change. It ships as x86-64 shared libraries (libcktso.so / cktso.dll, plus _L variants with 64-bit indices) and one header, cktso.h, with both a C API (CKTSO_CreateSolver, CKTSO_Analyze, CKTSO_Factorize, CKTSO_Refactorize, CKTSO_Solve, CKTSO_SolveMV) and a C++ abstract-interface instance. Input is CSR (unsorted column indexes and, since 20231101, duplicates allowed) in real or complex double, solved in row or column mode; it is not API-compatible with KLU, so adopting it means rewriting the solver glue.
how_it_is_fast: Ordering: it runs 10 fill-reducing orderings (8 minimum-degree variants, 2 nested-dissection variants) and keeps the one with the fewest predicted flops; the TCAD paper reports NICSLU's AMD-style ordering produces 39.8% and METIS-based PARDISO 188% more factorization flops than CKTSO's on 56 circuit matrices. Factorization: a pivoting-reduction 'fast factorization' reuses the previous pivot order and symbolic structure while checking each pivot, falling back to partial pivoting from the first bad row, which lets it parallelise like a refactorization. Solving: a structure-adaptive hybrid parallel forward/backward substitution, plus supernode detection and adaptive kernel selection, with AVX2 and FMA required.
when_to_use: SPICE-style transient or DC simulation on x86-64 with AVX2/FMA, where the same sparsity pattern is factorized hundreds of times and KLU's sequential refactorization dominates run time.

Large post-layout, power-grid or mesh-like circuit matrices, where its nested-dissection ordering cuts fill-in sharply versus AMD-based KLU or NICSLU (the paper names G3_circuit, G2_circuit, memchip, meg1 and FullChip).
Multi-core workstations (the paper uses a 16-core Xeon Gold 6130) where you want parallel factorization with KLU-style full-row threshold partial pivoting rather than a partitioned BBD approach.

Commercial or in-house simulators that can accept a binary dependency and want KLU-like call structure (analyze / factorize / refactorize / solve) with a separate GPU add-on (CKTSO-GPU) available later.
when_not_to_use: Anything that must be open source, auditable, rebuilt, or shipped on non-x86 hardware: only x86-64 Linux (CentOS 6/7, Rocky 8) and Windows binaries exist; Apple Silicon support is an open request (issue #3).
Deployments that cannot depend on a licence key: the library refuses to run (error -99) without license/cktso.lic next to the .so/.dll, and the shipped key carries an expiry date (2028-12-31).

One-shot solves or non-circuit matrices: analysis is slow by design (it races 10 orderings), the first factorization and first parallel solve are much slower than later ones, and the author says the implementation is tuned for circuit matrices; on several of the largest matrices MKL PARDISO factorized faster in the 2022 results PDF.
Single-precision, or complex-heavy workloads where speed matters: only double (real or complex) is offered and the user guide says complex performance is not yet fully optimised.

Projects needing responsive support: open issues on parallel slowdown on Windows (#12), thread auto-detection (#14), natural-ordering failures (#16) and a demo crash in an MSVC debug build (#18) have no maintainer replies.

integration.form: shared lib (prebuilt .so / .dll per platform) plus one C/C++ header; no source
integration.dependencies: none beyond the C/C++ runtime per the README; a licence key file cktso.lic must sit beside the library
integration.min_toolchain: Binaries built with gcc 4.8.2 (CentOS 6), gcc 4.8.5 (CentOS 7), gcc 8.5.0 (Rocky 8) and for Windows 7+ x64; the demos compile with g++ -O3 -std=c++11; the header also works from C99 (stdbool.h)
integration.platforms: x86-64 only, CPU must support AVX2 and FMA (CKTSO_CreateSolver returns -10 otherwise; CKTSO_CreateSolverNoCheck skips the check for VMs that hide the flags); Linux and Windows
integration.thread_safety: One solver instance owns a thread pool created at Analyze; the tips document says several instances may run in parallel only if each runs in its own thread, and one instance may handle several matrices in turn
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same analyze/factor/refactor/solve flow as KLU, but a different API, CSR (row) rather than KLU's CSC input unless column mode is selected, and a licence file to deploy

gotchas: Pass representative values (not NULL) to CKTSO_Analyze: with ax=NULL static pivoting is disabled and ordering is structure-only, which the tips document warns can increase fill-in dramatically.

Fast factorization (Factorize with fast=true) is unsafe after a big change in values: the tips say to disable it for the first factorization of each DC method or stepping value and after a time-step rollback.

Parallel solve needs a setup costing about 2-5x a sequential solve each time the LU structure changes, and the tips do not recommend parallel solve for column-mode matrices on Windows; the library may silently fall back to one thread based on matrix features (check oparm[18]).
Default threads=0 uses all physical cores as detected; the user guide recommends setting the count explicitly, and auto-detection in cloud VMs is reported as unreliable (issue #14).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick CKTSO over GSS (also binary-only, compared with an old PARDISO) or RSLAB (pure-Rust KLU-style solver measured against PARDISO) when the matrices come from SPICE and you can run on x86-64 with a licence key and want multi-core refactorization; pick PanguLU instead for distributed multi-GPU LU on general matrices, and stay with KLU when source access, portability or a sequential embedded build matters more than speed.
verified_claims_summary: The README's 'on average >3x faster than sequential KLU (AMD ordering) when sequential and >25x with 16 threads' on 66 SuiteSparse circuit matrices is first-party with no hardware or method; the 2022 results PDF (old version, Xeon Gold 6130 16 cores, gcc 4.8.5, KLU given NICSLU's ordering) shows about 2.8x and 14.6x. The author's IEEE TCAD 2025 paper, shipped in the repo as doc/tcad.pdf, compares only with NICSLU and oneMKL PARDISO on 56 circuit matrices on the same Xeon Gold 6130, mostly in the best case where fast factorization never re-pivots: 5.9x over NICSLU and 11.9x over PARDISO at 16 threads, about 20% lower when 10% of runs re-pivot. The shipped demo/benchmark.cpp likewise times 100 Factorize(ax, fast=true) calls on unchanged values, so its numbers are also that best case.
status_note: Actively updated (latest version 20260321, last commit 2026-03-26) but distributed as proprietary binaries with no licence text and a time-limited key, so it is a reference to call, not code to copy.
